I checked N = 0, 1, 2, 3, 10, 50 and 90, and got 1, 1, 2, 3, 89, 20365011074 and 4660046610375530309. I tested with the compilers installed here, not specifically rustc 1.75.0 and g++ 13.2.0. I deleted the test binaries afterwards, so only `main.rs` is in the folder.

**How it works:** Rust lets block comments sit inside other block comments, but C++ doesn't.

- **Line 1, `/* /* */`:** C++ sees a complete comment that ends on that line, so it compiles the C++ code below. Rust sees two comments opened and only one closed, so it treats the C++ code as part of a comment it is still inside.
- **`#if 0` then `*/`:** The C++ preprocessor skips everything after `#if 0`. The `*/` closes Rust's remaining comment, so Rust compiles the Rust `main` that follows.
- **End of file, `/* /* */`, `#endif`, `// */`:** These lines do the same thing in reverse. C++ sees the `#endif` and treats the final `*/` as part of a `//` line comment. Rust sees all of it as a comment, since `//` means nothing inside a block comment.

**Limits:**
- Both versions use 128-bit integers, so results are correct up to N = 184. Above that, the Rust build stops with an overflow error and the C++ build prints a wrong, wrapped-around number.
- `rustc` saves the binary in whatever folder you run it from, not next to the source file. So `rustc /tmp/.../polyglot/main.rs && /tmp/.../polyglot/main N` only works if you run it from inside `polyglot/`. Otherwise add `-o /tmp/.../polyglot/main` to the `rustc` command. Nothing in the source file can change this.
